title: Tier 1: Sensorimotor (~4–18 months)

html:
The "Reflex System" (Level 3) becomes a smooth, voluntary "Single Sensorimotor Action"; the skill is one coherent perception-action (sensorimotor) routine, like sustained looking or a simple grasp. Fischer’s example is an infant who can keep her gaze on a swinging doll-effective control of a single action, but not relations between actions. The child now operates on the physical world; Piaget noted that this is where infants become environmentally focused.

Level 1: Single Sensorimotor Set ( 3-4 months)

The child can perform a single, voluntary action on an object. They cannot yet coordinate two voluntary actions simultaneously. If they are busy looking at something, they might stop listening. If they are busy grasping, they might stop looking. A "set" refers to a cohesive, voluntary behavior pattern (a scheme) that the infant applies to a specific object or event.

Example 1: The Voluntary Grasp (The "Power Grip")

The infant sees a block, reaches for it, and wraps their fingers around it firmly.

In the Palmar Reflex, the hand closed only because the palm was touched; in this Sensorimotor Set, the infant initiates the grasping to hold the object.

The infant grasps the object but cannot manipulate it (turn it over, pass it to the other hand) while holding it. The hand simply "holds."

Example 2: Visual Inspection (The "Stare")

The infant locks their gaze onto a face or a high-contrast toy and studies it intently for several seconds. This is not just the Visual Tracking Reflex (following movement). This is active information gathering. The infant controls the duration and focus of the gaze.

The infant often seems "stuck" staring at the object (sometimes called "sticky fixation"). Because they are in a Single Set, they often cannot easily break their gaze to look at something else until the stimulus changes or they become exhausted.

Example 3: The "Bat" (Ballistic Striking)

The infant sees a mobile hanging above them and excites their arm to strike it, causing it to spin. An infant mobile task makes an action–outcome contingency visible (Figure) 1. Movement profiles are compared across connected and unconnected limbs (Figure).

This is a constructed action used to make an interesting event continue (a precursor to the "Secondary Circular Reactions" noted by Piaget; intentionally repeating actions that produce interesting effects in the external world, shifting focus from self (primary) to the environment).

The action is not fine-tuned. The infant cannot hit the mobile gently versus hard on command; they just run the "Hit" program.

Example 4: Non-Social Babbling (Vocal Practice)

The infant lies in the crib and produces a string of vowel sounds ("ooo-aaa") for the sheer sensation of making noise.

This is often done when the infant is alone or not focusing on anything else. If a parent enters and waves (visual stimulus), the infant often stops vocalizing immediately because they cannot maintain the Vocal Set while processing the new Visual Set.

Level 2: Sensorimotor Mappings ( 7-8 months)

The child coordinates two actions to achieve a goal. This is the beginning of "means-end" behavior; the dawn of intentionality.

Example 1: Pulling a blanket (Action A) to bring a toy resting on it within reach (Action B).

Action A: Pulling the blanket (Motor action).

Action B: Grasping the toy (Motor action).

Mapping: The child wants the toy but cannot reach it. They realize that "pulling the blanket" (Action A) causes the toy to come closer, allowing "grasping the toy" (Action B). They map the means to the end.

Example 2: Two-Handed Coordination (Container Play)

Action A: Stabilizing an object.

Action B: Manipulating the object.

Mapping: The child holds a box steady with the left hand (Action A) so the right hand can pull the lid off (Action B). In Level 1, the hands acted independently or mirrored each other; now they have distinct, complementary roles.

Example 3: Auditory-Motor Localization (The "Name Call")

Action A: Auditory processing (Identifying a specific meaningful sound, e.g., their name).

Action B: Motor orientation (Turning the body).

Mapping: The child hears their name spoken, processes the meaning, and maps it to the voluntary action of turning to look at the speaker.

Level 3: Sensorimotor Systems ( 11-13 months)

The child coordinates two or more Sensorimotor Mappings into a meaningful system. This allows them to compare multiple variables (e.g., "If I do X, Y happens; but if I do Z, Q happens") and vary their actions to solve new problems. This is the stage of active experimentation, corresponding to Piaget’s "Tertiary Circular Reactions" (i.e deliberately experimenting with objects and actions through trial-and-error to discover new outcomes and understand cause-and-effect). The child can hold Action A constant while varying Action B to see how the outcome (C) changes (A+ΔB→ΔCA + \Delta B \rightarrow \Delta C).

Example 1: The "High Chair Physicist"

The child is sitting in a high chair with a handful of peas or a spoon. They don’t just drop the object; they drop it differently each time.

Mapping A (Release): The mapping of opening the hand to letting the object fall (vertical drop).

Mapping B (Thrust): The mapping of arm extension force to horizontal distance.

The System:

First, they simply open their hand (Mapping A) and watch the spoon hit the floor directly below.

Next, they push the spoon gently (Mapping A + Low B) and watch it land a few inches away.

Finally, they throw it hard (Mapping A + High B).

They are testing the relationship between Force and Landing Position. They are systematically varying the initial velocity to learn the rules of trajectory.

Example 2: The "Sound Engineer" (Acoustics)

The child has a wooden spoon and is crawling around the kitchen hitting different surfaces.

Mapping A (The Strike): The motor action of swinging the arm to hit a surface.

Mapping B (Auditory Feedback): The processing of the resulting sound (pitch, timbre, volume).

The System:

The child hits the carpet (Mapping A applied to Surface 1) →\rightarrow Result: Dull thud (Low auditory feedback).

The child hits the metal pot (Mapping A applied to Surface 2) →\rightarrow Result: Loud clang (High auditory feedback).

The child hits the family dog or a parent (Mapping A applied to Biological Agent) →\rightarrow Result: Reaction/Noise.

The child is holding the action constant but varying the target surface to classify objects based on their material properties (acoustic resonance).

Example 3: The "A-not-B" Success (Object Permanence)

An object is hidden under Cloth A, then moved (while the child watches) under Cloth B. Related infant experiments make physical expectations visible (Figure) 2. The study measures differences in infants’ looking preferences (Figure).

Mapping A (The "Search A" Habit): The child remembers the object was at A and knows how to pull Cloth A to reveal it.

Mapping B (The "Visual Track"): The child visually tracks the object moving to location B.

The System:

In Level 2, these mappings compete. The child sees the object go to B, but the "Search A" mapping is so strong they look under A anyway (A-not-B Error).

Now, the child integrates them. The visual tracking (Mapping B) updates the search target. The child suppresses Mapping A and executes the search at B.

Example 4: The "Container" Fit (Volume & Orientation)

The child has a large container (like a bucket) and several smaller objects (a ball, a square block, a long stick).

Mapping A (Insertion): The motor action of placing an object inside a boundary.

Mapping B (Object Rotation): The manipulation of the object’s orientation in 3D space.

The System:

They drop the ball in (Easy fit).

They try to put the long stick in sideways (Mapping A). It hits the rim (Failure).

Instead of giving up, they rotate the stick vertically (Mapping B) and try Mapping A again (notice the coordination of mappings). It slides in.

They then try to put the bucket inside the cup (Size inversion).

They are testing spatial containment. They are learning the rules of "big vs. small" and how orientation affects whether one object can contain another.

Example 5: Social Referencing (The "Visual Cliff")

The child crawls toward a drop-off (or a scary toy) but pauses to look at their mother’s face.

Mapping A (Exploratory Drive): The child sees an interesting goal and initiates crawling toward it.

Mapping B (Emotional Interpretation): The child sees the mother’s fearful facial expression and maps it to "danger/stop."

The System:

The child does not just react to the toy or just react to the face. They treat the mother’s face as information about the environment.

They construct a system: "The toy is desirable (Mapping A), BUT Mom looks scared (Mapping B), therefore the toy is dangerous." The child halts based on the synthesis of these two inputs.

Example 6: Sequential Tool Use

The child uses a stick to retrieve a toy, but there is a barrier in the way requiring a maneuver.

Mapping A (The "Pull"): Mapping the stick movement toward the body to bring the toy closer.

Mapping B (The "Push/Slide"): Mapping the stick movement sideways or away to navigate around the obstacle.

The System:

A child in Level 2 creates a simple cause-effect: Pull Stick →\rightarrow Get Toy. If a barrier blocks the straight path, they fail.

Now, the child coordinates the mappings into a sequence: First Push/Slide (Mapping B) to clear the obstacle, then transition smoothly to Pull (Mapping A). They understand that an action moving away from the goal is sometimes necessary to achieve the goal.

Example 7: Complex Imitation (Gesture + Vocalization)

The parent claps their hands while saying "Yay!" and the child imitates the full performance.

Mapping A (Motor Imitation): Mapping the visual sight of clapping to the motor action of clapping hands.

Mapping B (Vocal Imitation): Mapping the sound of "Yay" to the vocal action of saying "Yay."

The System:

A child in Level 2 typically does one or the other. If they clap, they stop talking. If they talk, they stop clapping.

Now, they integrate the two mappings into a single performance. They can coordinate the rhythm of the hands (Mapping A) with the timing of the voice (Mapping B).
